Where symbols share a cell, the voiceless ones come first and the voiced follow the dot. Secondary articulation (ʷ ʲ ˠ ˤ) and length (ː) stay in the cell of the plain sound.

### Vowels

| | Front | Back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Close** | i iː | u uː |
| **Close-mid** | e eː | o oː |
| **Open-mid** |  | ɔ ɔː |
| **Near-open** | æ |  |
| **Open** | a |  |

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: long vowels oː eː uː ɔː iː. Nasality: no nasal vowels.

### Tone, syllables and stress

| tone | IPA | spelling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | a˨ | grave à |
| high | a˦ | acute á |

The language has 2 phonemic tones, marked on every vowel in the IPA here.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 33%, CVC 29%, CVCC 6%, V 4%, VC 3%. At most 1 consonant(s) before the vowel and 2 after it.
Stress falls on the next-to-last syllable. The IPA on this page marks it with ˈ before the stressed syllable.
Core words average 1.57 syllables (3.5 sounds); 15% of words share their form with another word.

### Phonological rules

Rules the language applies today, in order. A new sound change starts as a rule applying across words; as it ages it narrows to words, then to word-making, and in the end dies, leaving its alternations in single words.

| # | rule | applies | since | example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | f → v, fʲ → vʲ, p → b, pʲ → bʲ / _[+voice −son] | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~7 kyr ago | roː˦f + dʒi˨ → roː˦vdʒi˨ 'bone + hand (compound)' |
| 2 | f → ∅, fʲ → ∅, hʷ → ∅, hː → ∅ / V_C (compensatory lengthening: a fricative coda lost, the vowel lengthened) | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~7 kyr ago | roː˦f + -tsʲi˦ → roː˦tsʲi˦ 'bone-agent' |
| 3 | ɖ → r / #_ (a word-initial retroflex stop became r) | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~5 kyr ago | – |
| 4 | f → h / #_ | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~3.5 kyr ago | – |
| 5 | p → b, pʲ → bʲ, pʷ → bʷ, t → d / N_ | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | o˨u˨mʷ + ʔa˦lːi˦ʔ → o˨u˨mʷʔ̬a˦lːi˦ʔ 'fish (river) + be alive (compound)' |
| 6 | f → h / #_, V_V | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | roː˦f + -i˨ → roː˦hi˨ 'bone-cause' |
| 7 | x → h / #_ | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | – |
| 8 | ∅ → j / i_V | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | i˦ + -i˨ → i˦ji˨ 'arm or hand-cause' |
| 9 | V˨ → V˦ / _C*V˨ | across words in a phrase and inside words | ~19.5 kyr ago | pʲi˨f tɔː˨ → pʲi˦f tɔː˨ 'drink go' |
| 10 | /pʷ/ → [bʷ] / V_V | everywhere (an allophone: how a sound is said) | – | /mæ˨pʷeː˦li˦j/ → [mæ˨bʷeː˦li˦j] 'baby' |
| 11 | /tsʲ/ → [dzʲ] / V_V | everywhere (an allophone: how a sound is said) | – | – |
| 12 | /tɕ/ → [dʑ] / V_V | everywhere (an allophone: how a sound is said) | – | – |
| 13 | /s/ → [z] / V_V | everywhere (an allophone: how a sound is said) | – | /i˦su˦/ → [i˦zu˦] 'name:god:1261' |

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · mʲ ‹my› · mʷ ‹mw› · n ‹n› · nʲ ‹ny› · nʷ ‹nw› · nː ‹nn› · ȵ ‹ň› · ɲ̟ ‹ny› · p ‹p› · pʲ ‹py› · pʷ ‹pw› · b ‹b› · bʲ ‹by› · t ‹t› · tʲ ‹ty› · tː ‹tt› · d ‹d› · dː ‹dd› · ȶ ‹ť› ‹t› · ɖ ‹ḍ› ‹d› · ʔ ‹'› · ʔː ‹':› · ts ‹ts› · tsʲ ‹tsy› · tɕ ‹ć› ‹c› · tʃ ‹ch› · dʒ ‹j› · s ‹s› · sʲ ‹sy› · sʷ ‹sw› · ʃ ‹sh› · f ‹f› · fʲ ‹fy› · vː ‹vv› · θ ‹th› · x ‹kh› · hʷ ‹hw› · hː ‹hh› · ɻ ‹ḻ› ‹l› · j ‹y› · jː ‹yy› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · lː ‹l·l› ‹ll› · ɫ ‹ll› · ɭ ‹ḷ› · ɭʷ ‹ḷw› · r ‹rr› · rʲ ‹rry› · rʷ ‹rrw› · rː ‹rrr› · ǂ ‹ǂ› · ᵑʘ ‹npx›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · iː ‹ii› · u ‹u› · uː ‹uu› · e ‹e› · eː ‹ee› · o ‹o› · oː ‹oo› · ɔ ‹ọ› ‹o› · ɔː ‹ọọ› ‹oo› · æ ‹æ› ‹ae› · a ‹a›

Tones are written over the vowel: low grave à, high acute á (Yoruba-style).

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.
 Book folds that merge two sounds: ‹ť› is written ‹t›, ‹ḍ› is written ‹d›, ‹ḻ› is written ‹l›.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; noun before the numeral; relative clause before the noun. Overall it is head-final.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, a rich case system, nominative-accusative alignment, no grammatical number, a gender system based on sex.
Verbs mark past, future, perfective and progressive; there is an indirect (reported or inferred) evidential. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs agree with the subject by prefixes; not with the object.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; serial verbs; verb reduplication; a copula; adjectives that behave like verbs; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words left in place; a decimal counting base; a 'have' verb for possession.
Measured morphology: 20 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.6 (0 free word … 3 fused), 72 paradigm cells, 39 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns take 3 case markers: ablative (ABL): a suffix (soː˦, from 'leave'); dative (DAT): a clitic after the noun phrase (tæ˦, from 'give'); comitative (COM): a clitic after the noun phrase (æ˦, from 'with'). Adpositions (free words, not yet case): accusative (ACC): a separate word after the noun phrase (tʲi˦, from 'take'). Alignment is accusative: the object is marked (ACC), subjects are not.

| *nʲi˨-ji˨-soː˦* |
| --- |
| M-house-ABL |

‘from the house’

| *nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ=tæ˦* |
| --- |
| M-man=DAT |

‘to/for the man’

| *nʲi˦x-uː˦mʲi˦f* | *tʲi˦* |
| --- | --- |
| M-dog | ACC |

‘the dog (as object)’

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into genders by sex: class 1 for men, and by default most other nouns, a prefix (nʲi˨, from 'man').

| *nʲi˨-fi˨ʃ* |
| --- |
| M-father |

‘father’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Perfect (PRF): a suffix (m, from 'hold'); future (FUT): a suffix (ɫ, from 'want'). Unmarked: habitual (left to context).

| *tɔː˦-m* |
| --- |
| go-PRF |

‘(it) has gone’

| *tɔː˨-ɫ* |
| --- |
| go-FUT |

‘(it) will go’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Speakers mark how they know: reported (evidential) (REP): a separate word after the verb phrase (ʔo˦u˦ɫ, from 'say'). Mood markers: mirative (news, surprise) (MIR): a separate word after the verb phrase (mæ˨, from the perfect marker).

| *tɔː˨* | *ʔo˦u˦ɫ* |
| --- | --- |
| go | REP |

‘(it) goes, they say’

| *tɔː˨* | *mæ˨* |
| --- | --- |
| go | MIR |

‘(look!) it goes! (news to the speaker)’

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1SG: a prefix (ɔː˦, from 'I'); 2SG: a clitic before the verb (a˨j, from 'thou'); 2PL: a prefix (tɕi˦, from 'you'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there. No marker yet for 3SG, 3PL (zero). 1PL is shown by a change of the stem's vowel (see Word shapes).

| *ɔː˦-lɔː˨* |
| --- |
| 1SG-go |

‘I go’

| *a˨j=tɔː˨* |
| --- |
| 2SG=go |

‘you go’

| *tɕi˦-l* |
| --- |
| 2PL-go |

‘you all go’

**Negation.** Negation is a clitic before the verb phrase (ma˨f, from 'nothing').

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ta˦r* | *tʲi˦* | *ma˨f=ɔː˦-pʲi˨f* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-milk | ACC | NEG=1SG-drink |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words stay where the questioned phrase would stand: who i˦f, what ɔː˦, where tsʲi˦ʔɔː˦, when ȵa˦nːi˦ʔ, how na˨.

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-we˦* | *tʲi˦* | *a˨j=ʔa˦* | *tsʲe˦i˦ɫ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-thunder | ACC | 2SG=hear | Q |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-feː˦ri˦tsʲ* | *ɔː˦* | *tʲi˦* | *sʷo˦u˦ʔ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-child | what | ACC | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-me˨i˨ɻ* | *tʲi˦* | *ɲ̟a˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-fish | ACC | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with a 'have' verb ('my mother has a boat').

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *nʲi˦x-uː˦mʲi˦f* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-M-man | M-dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *a˦f* | *nʲi˨-ʔeː˦t* | *nʲi˨-nʷe˦* | *tʲi˦* | *dʒi˦ȵi˨* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | CL1-mother | M-boat | ACC | have |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause before the noun, no relativizer.

| *fa˨flɔː˦r* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-la˦r* |
| --- | --- |
| dance | DEF-CL1-woman |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a suffix (ʔ, from 'that'). Adjectives behave like verbs: 'the water is cold' is said as 'the water colds', with the verb's markers.

| *nʲi˨-tʲi˦* | *nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *nʲi˨-lɔ˦mtsʲ-ʔ* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M-that | M-man | M-merchant-COP |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-nʲi˦* | *ɲ̟a˦ʔ* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-M-water | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done intensely (INTS), by copying the stem's first consonant and vowel before it.

| *tɔː˨-tɔː˨* |
| --- |
| INTS-go |

‘(an action done intensely)’

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-me˨i˨ɻ* | *tʲi˦* | *ɲ̟a˨-ɲ̟a˨* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-man | DEF-M-fish | ACC | INTS-eat |

‘The man really eats the fish.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-me˨i˨ɻ* | *tʲi˦* | *ɫi˨ȵ* | *sʷo˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-man | DEF-M-fish | ACC | take | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *soː˨* | *tɔː˨* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** DAT is a case clitic, on the recipient.

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-la˦r* | *nʲi˨-me˨i˨ɻ* | *tʲi˦* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-feː˦ri˦tsʲ=tæ˦* | *ɔ˦ɫȵ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-CL1-woman | M-fish | ACC | DEF-M-child=DAT | give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is dʒi˦lːæ˦j and a hundred is ʔi˦ɫ.

| *ʔeː˦dʒi˦nːæ˨ɫ* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *mʲi˦ji˦nːæ˨ɫ* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *dʒi˦næ˦jːi˦j* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Concord.** The noun's class marker is copied onto demonstratives (agreement in class, as in Bantu and in Indo-European gender).

| *nʲi˨-tʲi˦* | *nʲi˦x-uː˦mʲi˦f* |
| --- | --- |
| M-that | M-dog |

‘that dog’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-juː˦mʲi˦f* | *ȵi˦* | *ʔɔ˦la˦ȵi˨* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-man | DEF-M-dog | sleep | say |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Word shapes.** The 1PL subject (we) is shown by a change of the stem's vowel (a˨ > a˦), its old ending long gone; the past is shown by a change of the stem's vowel (a˨ > a˦), its old ending long gone; the progressive is shown by a change of the stem's vowel (ɔː˦ > ɔ˦), its old ending long gone.

| *ɲ̟a˦* |
| --- |
| eat\1PL |

‘we eat’

| *ɲ̟a˦* |
| --- |
| eat\PST |

‘eat (past)’

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' eː˦ (near) and 'that' tʲi˦ (far).

| *nʲi˨-jeː˦* | *nʲi˦x-uː˦mʲi˦f* |
| --- | --- |
| M-this | M-dog |

‘this dog’

| *nʲi˨-tʲi˦* | *nʲi˦x-uː˦mʲi˦f* |
| --- | --- |
| M-that | M-dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** A conjoined comparison: 'A is big, B is small' (no comparative construction, as in many languages of New Guinea and Australia).

| *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-ɲ̟a˦ʔi˦bʲi˨ʔ* | *mæ˨n* | *tʲi˦-nʲi˨-juː˦mʲi˦f* | *feː˨ri˨n* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-M-man | big | DEF-M-dog | small |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 17 below)

Counting base: decimal. Several numerals began as other words: six = 'five one'; eight = 'four + two'; ten = 'two five'; twenty = 'ten two'.

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 13 families of 3+ words; 18% of the 743 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **stone** *tsʲiː˦bʲi˨ɭ* (N, coined 3.5 kyr ago in halfling 41); 4 words have it as their main root, 6 contain it.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are two themes from a closed pool, compounded (as Germanic *Wil-helm*, Slavic *Vladi-mir*); the byname is an inherited clan name. The tradition goes back to the halfling proto-language; it changed (order) in halfling 14. Themes: first eagle, horn, love, red, rich, sun, water, wolf; second king, mind, peace, shield, spear, strong.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **She'i'rryill** | /ʃe˦ʔi˦ʔrʲi˦ɫ/ | 'water-peace' | old, opaque | She'i'rryill 'water-peace': shei' 'water'; the root is now 'raining or rain' + rryill 'peace'; an old name, coined in d479 4.0 kyr ago as Sishrryiw |
| **Ipyiirryill** | /ʔi˦pʲiː˨rʲi˦ɫ/ | 'love-peace' | old, opaque | Ipyiirryill 'love-peace': ipyif 'love'; the word is gone from the language + rryill 'peace'; an old name, coined in d479 4.0 kyr ago as Ipyifrryiw |
| **Shibaswo'u'** | /ʃi˦ba˨sʷo˦ʔu˦ʔ/ | 'wolf-king' | old, opaque | Shibaswo'u' 'wolf-king': shibaliseerrifi 'wolf' + swou' 'king'; the root is now 'master'; an old name, coined in d479 4.0 kyr ago as Tsyipal'otsyi |
| **Shibarryill** | /ʃi˦ba˨rʲi˦ɫ/ | 'wolf-peace' | new | Shibarryill 'wolf-peace': shibaliseerrifi 'wolf' + rryill 'peace'; coined from today's words |
| **Jirrte** | /dʒi˦rte˦/ | 'eagle-mind' | new | Jirrte 'eagle-mind': jirr 'eagle' + te 'mind'; coined from today's words |

| **She'i'rryill Syithiysyiiňiw** | /ʃe˦ʔi˦ʔrʲi˦ɫ sʲi˦ði˨jsʲiː˨ȵi˨w/ | 'water-peace of the bear clan' | clan | the clan name Syithiysyiiňiw 'bear', from d479 4.0 kyr ago |

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
